package_info.package_manager: Windows Executable (PE file, distributed via ZIP archive)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is a Windows executable masquerading as a document (double extension), designed to harvest sensitive system and user information and exfiltrate it to attacker-controlled command-and-control (C2) servers. It performs no legitimate user-facing function and is solely intended for unauthorized data collection and exfiltration.

execution_context.file_location: Dropped executable (e.g., 'CMK Правила оформления больничных листов.pdf.exe')

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects basic system and user information (OS type, host name, user name), computes a unique client hash, and sends this data to a remote C2 server via HTTP POST with a custom cookie header.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting system and user information and exfiltrating it to an external server without user consent is a hallmark of infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate document or application would not collect and transmit system/user data to an unknown server.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise asset management tools may inventory system info, but with user/admin awareness and to trusted endpoints.
key_indicators: Execution on user launch of disguised executable

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects extended hardware and user data (BIOS info, CPU, RAM, desktop file list, network interfaces, registered usernames) and exfiltrates it to a remote C2 server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Harvesting detailed hardware and user data and sending it to an external server is not expected for any legitimate document or utility.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not enumerate hardware, user accounts, or desktop files and transmit them externally without user knowledge.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System inventory tools may collect such data, but only with explicit user/admin consent and to trusted infrastructure.
key_indicators: Enumeration of hardware and user data
Runs on execution of a file disguised as a document

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects comprehensive system, network, and software inventory data (disk space, domain, open ports, running processes, installed programs, system uptime, volume info) and exfiltrates it to a remote C2 server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting such a broad set of system and network information and sending it to an external server is highly indicative of reconnaissance for further attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not perform such extensive enumeration and exfiltration, especially when disguised as a document.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise management agents may collect similar data, but only with user/admin consent and to trusted endpoints.
key_indicators: Enumeration of running processes and open ports
Inventory of installed programs and user programs

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code encodes all collected system and user data in hexadecimal before exfiltrating it to the C2 server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Encoding exfiltrated data is a common anti-analysis and evasion technique in malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not obfuscate or encode telemetry data before sending it to unknown servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate telemetry may be encoded for protocol reasons, but not to untrusted endpoints.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code exfiltrates collected data to an internal IP address, likely for testing or evasion purposes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of internal IPs for C2 communication is highly unusual and suggests testing or attempts to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not send sensitive data to arbitrary internal IPs without user/admin configuration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Internal telemetry in enterprise environments, but only to known, trusted infrastructure.
key_indicators: C2 communication to internal IP addresses

attack_chain.action: User is lured into opening a ZIP archive containing a file with a double extension (e.g., .pdf.exe or .xls.exe), disguised as a document.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the malicious infostealer executable

attack_chain.action: Malicious executable runs and collects system, user, hardware, and network information from the victim's machine.
Collected data is optionally encoded (e.g., hex) for obfuscation.
Data is exfiltrated to a hardcoded C2 server or, in some variants, to an internal IP address for testing.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives victim data for reconnaissance or future attacks

behavioral_signatures: Execution of files with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe, .xls.exe) masquerading as documents
Enumeration of system, hardware, user, and network information immediately after execution
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded C2 domains or internal IPs with collected system data
Use of custom HTTP headers (e.g., Cookie: 3rd_eye=...) for victim identification
Encoding (e.g., hex) of exfiltrated data prior to transmission
file_indicators: Files with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe, .xls.exe) in user download or temp directories
Presence of executables with document icons
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to domains: shlalala.ru, ohmycars.ru, anime-clab.ru, glovatickets.ru (all /ch3ckState endpoints)
HTTP POST requests to internal IPs (e.g., 10.10.30.36, 192.168.21.182) on /ch3ckState
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of files with double extensions and document icons, especially those originating from ZIP archives. Detect processes that enumerate system, hardware, and user information immediately after launch. Inspect outbound HTTP POST requests to known C2 domains or internal IPs, particularly those containing system inventory data or using custom headers like '3rd_eye'. Flag exfiltration attempts where data is encoded (e.g., hex) prior to transmission. Correlate these behaviors to identify infostealer activity.
